summary: Garrett Galow, Head of Product at WorkOS, addresses authentication friction in MCP ecosystems. MCP's OAuth-based model requires individual consent for each server connection, breaking the single sign-on experience. This creates serious IT problems: lack of visibility into which MCP servers and AI agents employees use, inability to enforce access policies, and standing OAuth tokens that persist after SSO revocation or security incidents. The solution is Cross-App Access (XAA), where the identity provider acts as a trust bridge. In a demo, Claude Code with XAA connects to Figma automatically after a single Okta login, with no consent screen. The ID JAG flow involves four steps: (1) SSO login yields ID and refresh tokens; (2) the client requests an ID JAG token from the IDP using the refresh token, with the IDP verifying the user's membership in both client and resource applications; (3) the client presents the ID JAG token to the resource's authorization server, which validates it and issues a standard OAuth access token; (4) normal MCP communication proceeds. Steps two and three are invisible to the user. Access tokens are short-lived (approximately 5 minutes) but can be renewed automatically by rerunning the ID JAG flow as long as the SSO session remains active, improving security posture since revocation takes effect once tokens expire. Setup involves three parties: IT configures managed connections in the IDP (e.g., allowing Cursor to request access to Figma); MCP clients need an XAA-compatible SSO connection and must support the ID JAG token flow; MCP servers must support a new JWT bearer type, accept and verify ID JAG tokens against the IDP, and issue access tokens. WorkOS has built support for the client-side flow and handles SSO for Cursor and Anthropic. In Q&A, Galow clarifies that XAA addresses authentication only, not authorization—users receive their existing application permissions, and scoped access is being considered but not yet in the spec. The MCP client identifies target apps via audience URLs (e.g., mcp.figma.com). Currently only Okta supports XAA for OIDC-based connections, with SAML support planned; Microsoft Entra does not yet support XAA. Ecosystem challenges include protocol fragmentation, Entra's lack of DCR support, and limited adoption of the newer CIMD metadata standard.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Context
sections.summary: Garrett Galow introduces himself as Head of Product at WorkOS, which powers auth for Anthropic, Cursor, and OpenAI. The talk focuses on MCP authentication and the problem of repeated consent screens.

sections.title: The MCP Consent Screen Problem
sections.summary: MCP requires OAuth consent screens for every tool connection. Users must repeatedly click through consent, sometimes re-authenticating without knowing why. This is a relic of OAuth's design for mutually untrusting systems.

sections.title: IT and Security Challenges
sections.summary: MCP breaks the SSO model. IT lacks visibility into which MCP servers and AI agents employees use. Standing OAuth tokens persist after SSO revocation or incidents like the NPM Axios compromise, leaving security gaps. Onboarding requires repeated authentication management.

sections.title: Cross-App Access (XAA) Solution
sections.summary: XAA uses the IDP as a trust bridge between MCP client and server. Since both already trust the IDP (e.g., Okta), the IDP can broker credentials without manual consent.

sections.title: XAA Demo with Claude Code and Figma
sections.summary: Demo shows standard Claude Code requiring Figma consent, then XAA-compatible Claude Code performing one Okta login and automatically connecting to Figma with no consent screen.

sections.title: ID JAG Flow Explanation
sections.summary: Explains the four-step flow: SSO login yields ID and refresh tokens; client requests ID JAG token from IDP; client presents ID JAG to resource authorization server which issues a standard OAuth access token; normal MCP communication proceeds. Steps two and three are invisible to the user.

sections.title: Short-Lived Tokens and Security Posture
sections.summary: Access tokens are short-lived (~5 minutes) but auto-renewable via the ID JAG flow as long as the SSO session is active. If access is removed or the Okta session is locked, the user cannot reconnect once the token expires, improving security posture.

sections.title: Setup Requirements for IT, Clients, and Servers
sections.summary: IT admins configure managed connections in the IDP (e.g., allowing Cursor to request access to Figma). MCP clients need an XAA-compatible SSO connection and must support the ID JAG token request and exchange. MCP servers must support a JWT bearer type, accept and verify ID JAG tokens against the IDP, and issue access tokens. WorkOS has built client-side support and handles SSO for Cursor and Anthropic.

sections.title: Q&A and Ecosystem Discussion
sections.summary: Galow clarifies that XAA solves authentication only, not authorization—users get their existing app permissions with scoped access being considered for the future. The MCP client identifies target apps via audience URLs (e.g., mcp.figma.com) configured in the IDP. Currently only Okta supports XAA for OIDC connections; SAML support is planned. Microsoft Entra does not yet support XAA. Ecosystem challenges include Entra's lack of DCR support, protocol fragmentation across clients, and limited adoption of the newer CIMD metadata standard.

demonstrations: Standard Claude Code showing Figma MCP server requiring authentication via consent screen.
XAA-compatible Claude Code performing Okta SSO login once, then automatically connecting to Figma MCP server with no consent screen or manual clicks.
limitations: Many companies don't use SCIM, preventing full access revocation.
MCP OAuth tokens persist independently of IDP session revocation.
IT cannot determine which AI agents or MCP servers employees are using.
XAA addresses authentication only, not authorization; scoped access is not yet part of the spec.
Currently only Okta supports XAA, and only for OIDC-based connections; SAML support is planned but not yet available.
Microsoft Entra does not yet support XAA.
Entra does not support Dynamic Client Registration (DCR).
CIMD has very limited ecosystem support due to being only approximately three months old.
Protocol fragmentation exists across MCP clients in how they handle resource/scope parameters with Entra.
quantitativeClaims: Users may log into a half dozen or a dozen MCP servers.
Standing access tokens may persist for days, weeks, or even months after SSO revocation.
Most applications issue access tokens around 5 minutes, after which they expire but can be auto-renewed via the ID JAG flow.
SSO login frequency depends on IT policy—could be once a day or once a week.
CIMD metadata standard is approximately three months old.
